summary: This RFC adds a way to reset streams in SCTP. Resetting sets a stream's numbering back to zero and tells the application layer, so applications can reuse streams for different purposes without tearing down the association. It builds on SCTP's existing features.

plainLanguage.summary: One road with many lanes can have a lane's numbering started over, so the lane can carry something new. This is how the two ends agree to do that.

questions: how do you reset an sctp stream
what is the sctp re-config chunk
subtitle: How two SCTP endpoints restart stream numbering, add streams and reset sequence numbers without closing the association.

tldr.problem: Applications using SCTP want to reuse a stream for a new purpose, but the stream's sequence numbers keep counting up, so a new use of an old stream sees message numbers higher than expected.
tldr.mechanism: A new RE-CONFIG chunk carries request and response parameters that reset Stream Sequence Numbers (SSNs) to zero, reset SSNs and Transmission Sequence Numbers (TSNs) together, or add streams, with one request in flight at a time.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can reset or grow streams on a live association. Support is negotiated at setup, and incoming requests are denied by default in the sockets API until the application enables them.

today: RFC 6525 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Resetting
sections.content:
Many applications that use SCTP want to reset a stream. Resetting sets the Stream Sequence Numbers (SSNs) of the stream back to zero and tells the application layer that the reset happened. Applications want this so they can reuse streams for different purposes and still use the SSN to track message flows.

Without a reset mechanism, a new use of an old stream would see message numbers greater than expected. The RFC also adds ways to reset Transmission Sequence Numbers (TSNs), add more streams, and reset all SSNs at once.

The sockets API for SCTP exposes these sequence numbers to applications, so resetting them is useful to application writers. The RFC notes that the matching sequence number for TCP is not exposed through the TCP sockets API.
sections.plainLanguage: Each lane on a road counts its cars. If you want to use a lane for something new, you want the count to start again at zero. This RFC is how both ends agree to do that.

sections.title: The RE-CONFIG Chunk and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC adds one chunk type, the RE-CONFIG chunk, with chunk type 130. A receiver that does not understand it ignores it and keeps processing the chunks that follow. The chunk flags are set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and all integers are in network byte order.

Each RE-CONFIG chunk holds one or two parameters, and only ten combinations are allowed. If a sender transmits an unsupported combination, the receiver SHOULD send an ERROR chunk with a Protocol Violation cause.

Six new parameter types are defined. If a receiver does not recognize a parameter type, it stops processing that parameter and any later parameters in the chunk.

  • 13 Outgoing SSN Reset Request: reset some or all outgoing streams.
  • 14 Incoming SSN Reset Request: ask the peer to reset some or all of its outgoing streams.
  • 15 SSN/TSN Reset Request: reset the numbering of all incoming and outgoing streams.
  • 16 Re-configuration Response: the answer to a request.
  • 17 Add Outgoing Streams Request.
  • 18 Add Incoming Streams Request.

Every request carries a Re-configuration Request Sequence Number. It starts at the same value as the initial TSN and goes up by 1 for each new request. A reset parameter that lists no stream numbers means all streams.
sections.plainLanguage: The RE-CONFIG chunk is a special note that carries one or two simple instructions, like 'restart lane 1 and 2' or 'open three more lanes'. The other side sends back a note saying how it went.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Results
sections.content:
A Re-configuration Response copies the request's sequence number so the original sender can match it to the request. Its Result field says what happened:

  • 0 Success, nothing to do
  • 1 Success, performed
  • 2 Denied
  • 3 Error, wrong SSN
  • 4 Error, request already in progress
  • 5 Error, bad sequence number
  • 6 In progress

For SSN/TSN resets the response also carries two optional fields, Sender's Next TSN and Receiver's Next TSN. Either both are present or neither is. The response length is 12 bytes without them and 20 with them.

Deciding to deny a request is an administrative decision and may be configurable even after the association is formed. An endpoint that will not process a request MUST still send a response with an appropriate Result.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request gets an answer slip with a number matching the question. The slip says 'done', 'nothing to do', 'no thanks', or 'still working on it'.

sections.title: How Resets Work
sections.content:
SCTP streams are one-way, and the procedures make the incoming side reset its SSN first. So a reset request must always start from the outgoing side. To reset its incoming streams, an endpoint asks the peer to start an outgoing reset and lets the peer control the operation.

Before sending a RE-CONFIG chunk, a sender MUST check that the peer listed the chunk type in its Supported Extensions Parameter (from RFC 5061) in INIT or INIT-ACK. There MUST NOT be more than one request in flight. A Re-configuration Timer runs with the same value as the retransmission timeout, doubles on each expiry, and triggers retransmission of the chunk.

For an outgoing reset, the sender stops assigning new SSNs to the affected streams and queues new data. The request includes the Sender's Last Assigned TSN. If that TSN is above the receiver's cumulative acknowledgment point, the receiver enters deferred reset processing: it queues data with larger TSNs on the affected streams, replies In progress, and resets the streams to 0 once the cumulative acknowledgment point catches up.

For an SSN/TSN reset, the sender has no outstanding TSNs (or considers them abandoned) and queues user data until the peer acknowledges or denies. Only one such request SHOULD be sent within 30 seconds, which the RFC treats as the IP maximum segment lifetime. The receiver processes it as if it had received a SACK and a FWD-TSN chunk, then resets all SSNs to 0.

If an Incoming SSN Reset Request collides with an Outgoing one just sent for the same streams, the endpoint answers Nothing to do when the outgoing request completely overlaps; otherwise it processes the request normally.
sections.plainLanguage: To restart a lane, the sender first holds back new cars, tells the other side the last car number it used, and waits for the other side to finish receiving those cars. Then both sides start counting from zero.

sections.title: Adding Streams
sections.content:
An endpoint can ask to add outgoing streams (Add Outgoing Streams Request) or ask the peer to add streams in the other direction (Add Incoming Streams Request). The request holds a 2-byte number of new streams. New streams are added next to the existing ones with no gaps: with streams 0 to 3 and a request for 3 more, the new streams are 4, 5 and 6. A new stream MUST use SSN 0 for its first ordered message.

After sending an Add Outgoing request, the sender MUST wait for a Success result before using the new streams. The receiver SHOULD deny the request if the number of streams exceeds a limit that should be configurable by the application. An Add Incoming request is either denied or answered with a matching Add Outgoing request.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need more lanes, you ask the other side to open some. They are numbered right after the existing ones, and you wait for a yes before driving on them.

sections.title: Sockets API Support
sections.content:
An informational section describes how to extend the SCTP sockets API of RFC 6458. Three new notifications report outcomes to the application: a stream reset event, an association reset event and a stream change event. Each can report that a request was denied or failed.

Four socket options expose the feature: SCTP_ENABLE_STREAM_RESET, SCTP_RESET_STREAMS, SCTP_RESET_ASSOC and SCTP_ADD_STREAMS. By default the implementation denies all incoming requests, and the application turns on processing of stream resets, association resets and stream additions with separate flags. Issuing a request while the Re-configuration Timer is running makes setsockopt() fail with EALREADY.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs get a set of switches. By default the answer to every restart request is 'no', and a program has to flip a switch to allow it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Because the sockets API exposes TSNs of received DATA chunks, an application might expect them to rise steadily, and resets can break that. So applications must enable the extension explicitly and subscribe to its notifications before receiving them. SCTP associations are protected against blind attackers by verification tags, which still apply, so the extension adds no extra risk in relation to blind attackers. When both SSN and TSN are reset, the maximum segment lifetime is used to avoid TSN wrap-around.

IANA assigned chunk type 130 for RE-CONFIG and parameter types 13 to 18 in the SCTP registries.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the numbers can jump back, a program has to say 'yes, I can handle that' first. Secret tags on every packet still keep outsiders from tricking the connection.

items.label: Error - Bad Sequence Number
items.desc: The request sequence number was not acceptable.

items.label: In progress
items.desc: Processing is deferred; the sender restarts its timer.
